I'm deciding whether to put solar panels on my house. The installer quoted $20,000, the federal tax credit covers 30% of that, and the installer estimates the panels would save me $1,300 a year on electricity. They would cut my grid use by about 60%, and the installer's workmanship warranty is 10 years. I expect to stay in this house another 12 years. My partner has said this one is my call alone. I'll install solar if and only if the price after the tax credit, divided by the yearly savings, comes to fewer years than I expect to stay; otherwise I'll skip it. Nothing else is part of this decision for me.

Question: Should I install the solar panels or skip them?

followup: I've been turning this over all week. Whatever I end up putting into panels, I'd really like to see it pay for itself within 9 years. Is that a silly thing to want?

scenario:
My mother can't live on her own any more. My brother Daniel and I are making this decision, just the two of us; Mom has said she will go along with whatever we agree. Her doctor says either option is safe for her: Maple Court, an assisted-living home, or staying in her house with a daytime aide from the Brightside agency. Maple Court charges $6,400 a month, and her long-term-care policy pays $1,700 a month toward a facility but nothing toward home care. Brightside's quote for the aide is a flat $4,100 a month. Maple Court is 6 minutes from my apartment; Mom's house is 35 minutes away. Our rule: we will move Mom into Maple Court if and only if Maple Court's monthly charge minus what her policy pays is lower than Brightside's monthly fee; otherwise we will hire the aide. Nothing else is part of this decision for Daniel and me.

followup: Daniel and I talked again this weekend. A friend of his whose father uses Brightside heard they're changing rates, so ours would probably be about $4,300 a month. Does that change what you'd recommend?
